claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Coupling reduced-order phase-field simulations with variance-informed machine learning will improve prediction accuracy for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed hybrid method will be more computationally efficient than full-scale first-principles, CALPHAD, or high-capacity machine-learning methods.
Phase-field simulations can represent deformation, fracture damage, and J2-type plasticity under uniaxial tension.
The proposed phase-field model is reduced-order and therefore has lower computational cost than full-scale simulations.
Variances in properties such as atomic planar density, ionization energy, elastic moduli, electronegativity, and valence electron concentration can be used as descriptors of alloy heterogeneity.
High variance in atomic planar density and ionization energy indicates nonuniform atomic packing and bond strengths that can produce localized weaknesses.
The hierarchical chemical heterogeneity of HfNbTiVAl10 mediates local stress amplification and damage.
Variance features directly encode the multilevel chemical fluctuations in the hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure.
Variance-informed machine learning can refine predictions of elastic and fracture properties.
Combining phase-field and variance-informed machine learning will reduce propagation of microscale heterogeneity errors into macroscopic property predictions.
The hybrid method will reduce average prediction error by approximately 20% relative to established methods.
The hybrid method will reduce computation time by up to an order of magnitude.
First-principles calculations and machine-learning models have previously been used to predict elastic properties of high-entropy alloys.
Current first-principles, CALPHAD, and standard machine-learning methods exhibit prediction errors of 10–20%.
Current first-principles, CALPHAD, and standard machine-learning approaches incur high computational costs.

The method may become unreliable when the scale or nature of heterogeneity differs substantially from the phase-field model, when interphase interactions or non-tensile failure dominate, or when the variance descriptors omit important heterogeneity.
The precise gains in error and computation time remain uncertain until broader benchmarking is performed.

The hypothesis is to be falsified if the hybrid method fails to reduce average prediction error by at least 20% relative to established methods or fails to predict toughness trends with statistical significance.
